extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate students in mathematics or mathematical physics studying multivariable integration and vector analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter-level textbook guidance on double and triple integrals, special integrals (Beta/Gamma/Fresnel), and fundamental vector-analysis integral theorems (Ostrogradsky/divergence, Stokes/Ampère/Green). Presents definitions, conditions of applicability, and calculation techniques (coordinate choices, reductions, recursion/formula relations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of a surface integral to an integral over its projection
rubrics_metrics.description: When a curved surface S projects horizontally on a planar region C (plan of xy), the surface element dS relates to the projected element dσ by dS = dσ / cos(N,z) or equivalently dσ = dS cos(N,z), where (N,z) is the acute angle between the tangent (normal) and the z-axis. Hence a surface integral ∫_S φ dS can be reduced to a double integral over the projection: ∬_C φ(x,y) cos(N,z) dσ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when the surface projects to the xy-plane (projection limited by curve C) and when φ is specified at each point of the surface. Compute cos(N,z) as a function of x and y using the surface's tangent plane; then integrate over the planar domain with rectangular or polar coordinates as convenient. (Text gives explicit derivation and examples using polar coordinates and projections.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of integrand for existence of surface integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: If φ is a continuous function (having a determined value at every point) on the surface, the surface integral defined as the limit of Riemann-type sums exists and can be expressed as the corresponding double integral over the projection multiplied by cos(N,z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook constructs the integral by dividing the surface into infinitesimal elements and summing φ·dS; continuity ensures the Riemann-sum limit. Use the projection method and coordinate transforms for practical computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of coordinates when computing double/surface integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: Double and surface integrals may be computed using rectangular (x,y) coordinates or polar coordinates (r,θ) in the plane of projection; when switching to polar, include the Jacobian factor r (and the cos(N,z) factor for surface integrals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the coordinate system that simplifies the projection region (e.g., circular symmetry → polar). The text illustrates evaluating a spherical-surface-related integral by taking polar coordinates in the xy-plane and integrating r·dr·dθ with appropriate limits. Always include the correct differential area element (dx dy = r dr dθ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eulerian integral of the first kind (Beta function) B(a,b): definition and parameter conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: B(a,b) = ∫_0^{π/2} (sin u)^{2a-1} (cos u)^{2b-1} du (or other equivalent integral representations). The integral has meaning (is finite) when a>0 and b>0; it becomes infinite if either parameter is zero or negative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties noted: symmetry B(a,b)=B(b,a); use substitutions (e.g., u = sin t) to transform forms. Reduce computations to single-parameter integrals when possible. The text shows transformations that reduce B to integrals depending on a single parameter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eulerian integral of the second kind (Gamma function) Γ(a): definition and basic properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Γ(a) (denoted r(a) in the text) is defined by Γ(a)=∫_0^∞ u^{a-1} e^{-u} du for a>0. It satisfies the recursion Γ(a) = (a-1) Γ(a-1); Γ(1)=1. Γ(a) is infinite when a≤0 at singular points (e.g., Γ(0) = ∞). For positive integers n, Γ(n) = (n-1)!.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repeated application of the recursion to reduce computation to a parameter in (1,2] for which values are tabulated or known (e.g., Γ(1/2)=√π). Beware that Γ(a) diverges at nonpositive integers. The text gives integration-by-parts proof of the recursion and examples of values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beta–Gamma relation (connection between B(a,b) and Γ)
rubrics_metrics.description: B(a,b) = Γ(a) Γ(b) / Γ(a+b), derived by evaluating a suitable double integral (volume) in Cartesian and polar coordinates and equating the two expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute the same volume V by iterated integrals in different coordinate systems to derive the identity. Use recursion properties of Γ to reduce parameters when using numerical tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameter restrictions and divergence behavior for Eulerian integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: Both Beta and Gamma integrals require positivity of parameters for finiteness: B(a,b) finite iff a>0 and b>0; Γ(a) finite for a>0 and infinite when a=0 or a is a nonpositive integer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying formulas, ensure parameters satisfy these conditions. Use recursion relations to translate parameters into the convergent range before consulting tables or evaluating numerically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of Fresnel integrals by double-integral comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrals ∫_0^∞ cos(x^2) dx and ∫_0^∞ sin(x^2) dx can be evaluated by interpreting them as slices of a volume whose value is computed twice: once in rectangular coordinates (yielding the product of one-dimensional integrals) and once in polar coordinates (leading to an integral with cos and sin composition), then equating the two results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The method: construct an appropriate surface z = e^{-y^2} cos(x^2) (or related), compute the volume over the positive quadrant first by integrating in x then y (giving an expression involving the Fresnel integral), and second by polar coordinates (leading to an integral that can be evaluated); equate to solve for the Fresnel integrals. The textbook demonstrates this technique in detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and practical computation of triple integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: A triple integral over a volume V is the limit of sums ∭_V φ(x,y,z) dV obtained by decomposing V into infinitesimal parallelepipeds dx dy dz. Practically, reduce ∭ to an iterated integral by choosing an order of integration (e.g., integrate first in z with limits z1(x,y) to z2(x,y) giving a function f(x,y), then compute ∬ f(x,y) dx dy over the projection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decompose volume into stacks (piles) parallel to an axis to integrate first with respect to that coordinate. The limits of inner integrals are functions of the outer variables (determined by the surface equations). You may change integration order (integrate in x or y first) depending on convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergence theorem (Ostrogradsky formula) — hypotheses and statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Let F = (X,Y,Z) be a vector field defined in a continuous region of space whose components are continuous and admit first partial derivatives. For a volume V bounded by a closed surface S (with outward normal), the theorem states ∭_V (∂X/∂x + ∂Y/∂y + ∂Z/∂z) dV = ∬_S (X a + Y β + Z γ) dS, i.e., triple integral of divergence equals surface integral of flux outward through S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof in the text proceeds by first proving partial formulas for each coordinate (assuming at most two intersections with lines parallel to axes) and summing them; then extend to general surfaces. Ensure the field has required smoothness. Applications include computing volumes by surface integrals (e.g., set X=Y=0, Z=1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of divergence and flux
rubrics_metrics.description: Divergence div F is the scalar ∂X/∂x + ∂Y/∂y + ∂Z/∂z. The elemental flux through a surface element dS with outward normal N (with direction cosines a,β,γ) is (X a + Y β + Z γ) dS; the total flux through S is ∬_S (F·n) dS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use divergence to relate local expansion/compression of field to net outward flux via the divergence theorem. Keep track of orientation: outward normals give positive flux contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and components of curl (tourbillon)
rubrics_metrics.description: The curl (tourbillon) of a vector V is the vector ω with components given by differences of partial derivatives: ω_x = ∂Z/∂y - ∂Y/∂z, ω_y = ∂X/∂z - ∂Z/∂x, ω_z = ∂Y/∂x - ∂X/∂y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The curl appears in Stokes' theorem and in characterizing conservative fields. The text introduces it as preparation for plane and surface integral relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of a field normal to a family of surfaces (analytic integrability condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A field F = (X,Y,Z) is normal (colinear) at each point to a family of surfaces U(x,y,z)=C if there exists a scalar A(x,y,z) such that X = A ∂U/∂x, Y = A ∂U/∂y, Z = A ∂U/∂z. Analytically, this means the differential form A^{-1} (X dx + Y dy + Z dz) is an exact differential dU, and integrability conditions (equality of mixed partial derivatives) must hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook shows that the existence of such A is equivalent to the differential expression becoming a total differential (i.e., integrability conditions). It notes necessary conditions (relations among partial derivatives) and that there exist infinitely many factors A making the expression exact if (11) holds; the demonstration of sufficiency is omitted but the criterion is emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition for a field to be gradient (conservative field)
rubrics_metrics.description: A vector field derives from a scalar potential (is conservative) iff the differential form X dx + Y dy + Z dz is an exact total differential. Equivalently (under the smoothness assumptions given), the mixed partial derivative equalities must hold: ∂X/∂y = ∂Y/∂x, ∂Y/∂z = ∂Z/∂y, ∂Z/∂x = ∂X/∂z; equivalently the curl is zero everywhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When these conditions hold, one can find a potential function V with F = ∇V (the book sets the integrating factor A = 1 in this special case). The text emphasizes that vanishing curl is necessary and sufficient (within the framework of the chapter) for the field to derive from a potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stokes/Ampère (planar form) — hypotheses and formula
rubrics_metrics.description: For a planar vector field F = (X(x,y), Y(x,y)) with components continuous and with continuous first partial derivatives on a region, and for any simple closed contour C bounding area S, the theorem states ∬_S (∂Y/∂x - ∂X/∂y) dS = ∮_C (X dx + Y dy), where the line integral around C is taken in the positive (counterclockwise) sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook proves the plane formula by integrating first with respect to x or y on vertical/horizontal slices and then summing; it also derives the planar Stokes/Ampère relation from the 3D divergence theorem by applying it to a thin cylinder. Keep orientation consistent (positive sense for boundary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Green's theorem and its proof technique via cylinder
rubrics_metrics.description: Green's theorem (a special case of Stokes in the plane) is derived by constructing a thin cylinder above the planar region and applying the 3D divergence theorem to that cylinder; the lateral surface contribution gives the line integral while the bases cancel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this limiting-cylinder argument to relate planar area integrals of derivatives to contour integrals. The text gives the decomposition of the surface integral into base and lateral contributions and recovers the planar formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of numerical tables for Γ and B functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerical tables (e.g., tables of Γ(x) for x between 0 and 1) are available to compute values of Γ and B; reduce parameters using the recursion Γ(a)=(a-1)Γ(a-1) to bring arguments into the tabulated range (commonly 1 to 2) before looking them up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text references numerical tables (Houël) giving Γ values for x in [0,1]; use the recursion relations to shift parameters into the tabulated interval. Also use the Beta–Gamma relation to compute B from Γ values.
